questions.q: Name the three structural genes of the lac operon and the specific enzyme each encodes.
questions.a: Correct: lacZ encodes β-galactosidase (cleaves lactose to glucose + galactose), lacY encodes lactose permease (transports lactose into cell), lacA encodes thiogalactoside transacetylase (detoxifies non-metabolizable lactose analogs). A wrong answer (e.g., "lacZ makes permease" or missing lacA) reveals confusion between gene identity and enzyme function — a common board exam error where students swap Z and Y roles or omit lacA entirely, losing 1-2 marks in diagram-labeling questions.

questions.q: Explain why the lac repressor protein binds to the operator in the absence of lactose but releases when allolactose is present. Include the structural change involved.
questions.a: Correct: The lacI gene product (repressor) has two domains — an N-terminal DNA-binding domain (helix-turn-helix) that recognizes the operator sequence, and a C-terminal allosteric domain that binds allolactose. Without inducer, the repressor dimer binds operator, physically blocking RNA polymerase progression. Allolactose binding induces a conformational change that reduces DNA-binding affinity ~1000-fold, causing repressor release. A wrong answer stating "lactose binds repressor directly" (instead of allolactose) or "repressor degrades" reveals misunderstanding of allosteric regulation and the role of β-galactosidase in producing the true inducer — a NEET trap where 60% of students choose "lactose" as the inducer in MCQs.

questions.q: Predict the relative expression level of lac genes (high/low/zero) in *E. coli* grown in: (a) glucose only, (b) lactose only, (c) glucose + lactose, (d) neither sugar. Justify each prediction using both regulatory mechanisms.
questions.a: Correct: (a) Glucose only: LOW — repressor bound (no allolactose), CAP-cAMP absent (high glucose → low cAMP). (b) Lactose only: HIGH — allolactose removes repressor, low glucose → high cAMP → CAP-cAMP activates transcription. (c) Glucose + lactose: LOW — allolactose removes repressor BUT high glucose → low cAMP → no CAP-cAMP activation (catabolite repression). (d) Neither: ZERO — repressor bound, no CAP-cAMP. A wrong answer predicting HIGH in (c) reveals failure to integrate positive control — students often think "lactose present = operon ON" ignoring glucose override. This is the #1 board exam error in case-based questions on lac operon.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the lac operon (inducible) and trp operon (repressible) in terms of: (i) default state, (ii) effector molecule, (iii) effector action on repressor, (iv) metabolic logic.
questions.a: Correct: (i) lac default OFF (repressor bound), trp default ON (repressor inactive). (ii) lac effector = allolactose (inducer), trp effector = tryptophan (corepressor). (iii) allolactose INACTIVATES repressor → transcription ON; tryptophan ACTIVATES repressor → transcription OFF. (iv) lac: catabolic pathway — make enzymes only when substrate available; trp: anabolic pathway — make enzymes only when end product scarce. A wrong answer reversing the default states or calling tryptophan an "inducer" shows lack of conceptual framework for negative feedback vs. substrate induction — a frequent 3-mark board question where students lose marks for incomplete comparison tables.

questions.q: A student claims: "CAP-cAMP complex binds to the lac promoter and directly recruits RNA polymerase, so it is a transcription factor." Evaluate this statement. Is CAP-cAMP a transcription factor? Explain the precise molecular mechanism.
questions.a: Correct evaluation: The statement is PARTIALLY correct but imprecise. CAP-cAMP IS a transcription factor (activator), but it binds to the CAP site (upstream of promoter, centered at -61.5), NOT the promoter itself. It recruits RNA polymerase via protein-protein interaction between CAP's activating region 1 (AR1) and the α-subunit C-terminal domain (α-CTD) of RNA polymerase, stabilizing the closed complex and promoting isomerization to open complex. A wrong answer saying "CAP binds promoter" or "CAP works without RNA polymerase" reveals confusion between promoter-proximal elements and upstream activating sequences — a JEE Advanced level distinction where precise binding site location matters for footprinting assay interpretation.

questions.q: Design a genetic experiment using *E. coli* mutants to prove that the lacI gene product acts in trans (diffusible) while the operator acts in cis (DNA-bound). Specify the genotypes, expected phenotypes, and conclusion.
questions.a: Good answer criteria: Use partial diploids (F' plasmids). Test 1: F' lacI⁺ lacO⁺ lacZ⁺ / lacI⁻ lacO⁺ lacZ⁻ → if lacZ expressed only when inducer added, lacI⁺ acts in trans (repressor diffuses). Test 2: F' lacI⁺ lacOᶜ lacZ⁺ / lacI⁺ lacO⁺ lacZ⁻ → if lacZ on chromosome (O⁺) is inducible but plasmid (Oᶜ) is constitutive, operator acts in cis (Oᶜ mutation only affects linked genes). Conclusion: Trans-acting factor = diffusible protein; cis-acting element = DNA sequence. A poor answer using only haploid mutants or not distinguishing cis/trans reveals inability to design complementation tests — a standard molecular genetics approach tested in CUET and NEET.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The lac operon is an inducible ______ gene regulation system in *E. coli* that controls the metabolism of lactose through three structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA) under a common promoter and operator, regulated by a repressor protein encoded by the lacI gene and modulated by the inducer allolactose and the catabolite activator protein (CAP)-cAMP complex for glucose-dependent control.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you eat a bowl of kheer (rice pudding with milk) — your gut bacteria ______ encounter lactose but no glucose.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can diagram the lac operon with all components labeled, explain the molecular events when lactose is absent/present and glucose is absent/present, predict the expression level of lac genes in four metabolic conditions, and distinguish between negative control (repressor) and positive control (CAP-cAMP) mechanisms.
